Edwin:

There's also several comic-book themed novels not tied to the mainstream continuity, of which the best-known is " Soon I Will Be Invincible".

I must strongly urge you to not actually read "Soon I Will Be Invincible."  It has clever prose, and so there's lots of great-sounding quotes floating around out there, but I have seldom been more let down by a "climax".

However, there are certainly lots of classic comic book stories adapted into novels.  The only one I have read (and can therefore recommend) is Kingdom Come, but that would be a lot less fun without knowing the continuity behind it.  I do hear rave reviews about "It's Superman!" though.

Really, I think the easiest way to pick up some comics continuity and see a wider assortment of characters without actually reading comics is probably the animated adaptations - Justice League Unlimited, Brave And The Bold, Young Justice, and Avengers Earth's Mightiest Heroes all made points of showcasing some more obscure characters from their respective continuities in different ways, and all of them are good shows (though I could not personally get into YJ's first season) - Wolverine And The X-Men and Ultimate Spiderman also tread some obscure ground, though I think each has big flaws.

… not sure if any of those have Moon-Knight in them, now that I think about it.  But they will give you multiple takes each on Blue Beetle and Iron Fist, so you're getting what's really important.

EDIT: Wow, that drifted off-topic, even for me.  Regarding Empyreon, I think it would be amazing (and very Jack Kirby) for the space laserdude and the dark angel to be on the same team, or at least come from the same source.  Thusfar, however, SotM has kept its magic and its sci-fi pretty carefully separate, so I assume they shall continue in that vein.

What makes you say that would be Kirby-esque? Not arguing, just really curious. I have a lot of speculation tied up in that connection, anything you can share would be awesome.

Simple - Jack Kirby designed Marvel's version as Asgard.  In it, there was Heimdal, who looked like this:

That is to say, a man in armor, with a horned helmet, a shield, and a sword.

There was also Odin, who looked like this:

356×536 66.7 KB

That is to say, like a disco-themed Rorschach test, somehow made ambulatory by the cyborg spider atop its head.

Thus, when you think to mix Empyreon with a fairly traditional-looking angel, I think of Jack Kirby's ability to mix the familiar and the bafflingly insane, and treat it all as one coherent whole.

And you know what?  With a good creator at the helm, it really can be such a whole.

posts.cooked: Having read a rather bad trade of 1980s Green Lantern this afternoon, I find myself sympathetic with anyone who doesn't really want to read comics books.  They are often not held to high quality standards in writing, though the art is usually quite excellent, and I think of that as being more the point of a lot of comics.  There are certainly exceptions, the brilliant Neil Gaimans and Kurt Busieks of the world, writing their Kingdom Comes and their V for Vendettas; those are certainly literary achievements.  But there's also embarassingly awful soap opera and sci-fi so soft you could sink into it like quicksand, both in far larger quantities than the occasional excellence.  Carelessly wading in and reading just any old thing is a pretty sure recipie for having your intelligence insulted.

This will probably deserve a moderator split, soon, but I've been doing Supers in novels as a thing for a bit (actually - supers as novels in audiobook format- it's a long commute) and here's what I've read:

Soon I Will Be Invincible - which I enjoyed more than Ironic. While the ending wasn't everything I could have hoped for, it covered the character beats I needed to see. I will grant that it didn't end like a comic.

The "Ex-" series, Ex-heroes, Ex-patriots... Super hero after the zombies win fiction. You have to like both genres to like the series, I suppose, so I haven't picked up the third book, yet.

"Valveteen vs." I kinda love. At it's shallowest reading, the book is a series of silly short stories about a young woman who's power of making toys come to life was great as a teen hero, not so much as a twenty-something. At a deeper level, it is about how media chews through teen celebrities, and the costs associated with being one. I wish there were fewer f bombs I it so I could read it as a cautionary tale to my 4 year old in a couple of years.

Has anyone read Steelheart?

posts.name: Ironic
posts.cooked:
Amnachaidh:

Has anyone read Steelheart?

Oh man, have I.

Bias Warning: Brandon Sanderson is my favorite living novelist.  His Mistborn Trilogy is my favorite fantasy series of all time.  And for all that it becomes more of a Cliche with each Invincible and Irredeemable we see, I am a sucker for a Bad Superman story*.  Clearly, I am predisposed to think Steelheart is good.

But in my defense, it really is quite good.  It's a great look at how scary being a "badass normal" is from the ground, it may be the best example I know for having a character fresh out of their normal life surrounded by craziness without making them a bland Everyman, and Steelheart himself is an especially sinister and scary Bad Superman.

It does have its flaws - most notably Sanderson's need to write sequel hooks into everything he does shines through.  But I like it best as a standalone book, and it certainly holds up as such.  I recommend it strongly, needless to say.

Ironic

 

* I mean that figuratively - stories about a Supermanlike figure who is also a bad guy.  Not stories about Superman himself which are bad - those are even more common, and not so enjoyable.

posts.name: Edwin
posts.cooked:
Reckless:

Is there another medium that you find has a better track record?

It might be an apples and oranges comparison, but in general the small subset of movies based on comic books (as opposed to all of Hollywood) has something close to a 50/50 excellence/crap ratio, instead of the 10/90 that comics as a whole probably boils down to.  The Raimi Spider-Mans were fairly terrible, as were the third and fourth Batman movies, Green Lantern's not great, Daredevil was slightly tepid and Elektra was just ridiculous, the old Superman tetralogy (and its unofficial fifth entry, Superman Returns) vary from decent to awful, Sly Stallone's Judge Dredd was fun IMO but definitely not exactly good, and of course there was that 1994 The Punisher which was just a Rambo clone that claimed to be comics-based.  But conversely, you have Iron Man, Thor, both Hulk movies (the Ang Lee one was weird as heck but I considered it still reasonably good), Batman Begins and to a lesser Extent The Dark Knight (really, only Joker was much good in that one, but he counts for a lot), and for a very tenuous qualifier, The Incredibles.  I haven't seen Iron Man 2 and 3, The Avengers, the new Punisher or Dredd movies, Amazing Spider-Man or Man of Steel, but I've heard that most of these were well-reviewed.   So overall, if we grouped these movies into "great", "okay", and "bad", the piles would be roughly equal in size.  Whereas doing the same to comics would result in about a bookshelf or two worth of "great", a few truckloads of "okay", and a very literal mountain of absolute dreck (most of the absolute dreck titles you've probably never even heard of; I've found samplings of quite a few in the bargain bin of various comic stores, and wanted my dime back).

It's kind of an unfair comparison since the movies are generally based on the handpicked best (or at least okayest) of the comics.  But it works; Marvel Movies is batting about 900 from what I hear (I can personally confirm about half of it; the only one of the post-IM movies which I found slightly less than good was Incredible Hulk, and even that was pretty decent), and pretty much anything written by David S. Goyer is awesome.  Now if only someone would handpick the best of Hollywood's movies and turn them into usually-excellent comics…

posts.name: Silverleaf
posts.cooked:
People are assuming that I'm saying things which I'm absolutely not saying.

I didn't say that comics aren't literature. I said that comics aren't books, twice, but novels would certainly have been a better word. Comics aren't novels.

I didn't say that books can't have pictures. I said that the information in books (should have said novels) is primarily conveyed through the words. If you read the book out loud to someone they understand the majority or all of it without actually seeing the pages. Many children's books with pictures fall into this category too - the pictures are nice, and add to the enjoyment and may provide some extra info, but aren't strictly necessary for delivering the story. The Very Hungry Caterpillar still works if you can't see it, even though it's less fun that way.

With comics, the pictures are vital. And that's the distinction I'm making.

I was reading the kind of children's books that have only occasional pictures and have chapters and such with only minimal "I've never heard this word before because I'm five and I don't know what it means" assistance at five too. My parents used to read to me and taught me my letters and how they made up words before I went to "proper" school and so I learned to read earlier than most of my classmates. My school used those reading scheme type books mentioned, the first of which I remember very clearly had pictures of various acts in a circus, with the word "Look" on each page and nothing else. I thought that was completely pointless as a learn-to-read exercise for me, and said as much (my teachers loved my intelligence, but weren't fond of my outspokenness). That book? It was a comic, essentially, and not a book.

Maybe my dislike for the comic form stems from being encouraged to read books with fewer pictures and more words as a child - at seven I was reading about paleontology and natural history, spent all my pocket money and birthday money on books and shunned anything that was "for babies" and had more pictures than words, because the enjoyment for me was increased if I had to work to get it. Now I know that much of the comic form is aimed at adults, but I can't help letting my childhood prejudice colour my judgement. That child would say that comics are too easy and therefore less fun. The adult me is hopefully a bit more subtle than that, but the feeling is essentially the same. 

I'm very glad your daughter likes reading so much, and that you're doing so much to encourage her. That's wonderful. :)
